seasons.name: Tamaracks turn gold
seasons.note: Western larch, the conifer that drops its needles, glows orange on eastern hillsides.
seasons.evidence: In late September, they begin turning greenish gold. By early October, they're orange.

seasons.name: First frost on the lawns
seasons.note: Spokane's median first 32°F night falls around October 7.
seasons.evidence: NWS Spokane sorted first-freeze dates (143 years): median 10-07, range 09-10 to 11-11

seasons.name: Ducks and geese crowd Turnbull
seasons.note: Up to 30,000 ducks and geese stop over on Cheney's marshes in fall migration.
seasons.evidence: Up to 30,000 ducks and geese and several hundred Tundra Swans stop over during both spring and fall migration. (FWS: fall migration from September through November)

seasons.name: Rough-legged hawks come south
seasons.note: Arctic-nesting hawks arrive to hunt Palouse and West Plains fields all winter.
seasons.evidence: A few southbound birds are seen as early as mid-August, but they are not common until mid-October.

seasons.name: Tundra swans pass over
seasons.note: Swans rest on eastern Washington wetlands on their way to winter grounds.
seasons.evidence: autumn migration in eastern Washington ... mid-October to mid-November

seasons.name: Clocks fall back
seasons.note: Daylight saving time ends Sunday, November 1, and evenings go dark early.
seasons.evidence: daylight saving time ... ends on the first Sunday in November

seasons.name: Nights stay below freezing
seasons.note: November's normal low is 30°F, so most nights now freeze.
seasons.evidence: November: High 42°F / Low 30°F (1991-2020 averages)

seasons.name: Whitetail bucks in rut
seasons.note: Deer move all day during the rut and cross roads at dusk, so drive with care.
seasons.evidence: deer are especially active in November as the rut (mating season) is at its peak

seasons.name: First snow in the city
seasons.note: Spokane's first measurable snow usually comes by mid-November.
seasons.evidence: it typically it arrives in Spokane by Nov. 15

seasons.name: Inversion fog settles in
seasons.note: Cold air gets trapped in the valley, bringing gray days and freezing fog.
seasons.evidence: November through January is peak season for this atmospheric marvel

seasons.name: Kokanee gather to spawn
seasons.note: Kokanee, a landlocked sockeye, crowd Wolf Lodge Bay on Lake Coeur d'Alene to spawn.
seasons.evidence: Each winter from November as late as February, the landlocked small sockeye salmon called kokanee gather by the thousands to spawn.

seasons.name: Waxwing flocks descend
seasons.note: Bohemian waxwings from the north pass through towns eating berries.
seasons.evidence: Most Bohemian Waxwings in Washington are northern breeders that come down into Washington in winter. (Uncommon Oct, Fairly Common Dec)

seasons.name: December snows deepen
seasons.note: December is Spokane's snowiest month, averaging 13.8 inches.
seasons.evidence: December is Spokane's snowiest month with an average of 13.8 inches of snow (1991-2020)

seasons.name: Lifts turn on Mount Spokane
seasons.note: The ski park aims to open in early December if the snow allows.
seasons.evidence: Officials at Mount Spokane planned to open Dec. 7 with the caveat that the hill could open sooner if enough snow arrived.

seasons.name: Birders count the winter
seasons.note: The Christmas Bird Count opens December 14, and Spokane and Cheney groups count in the field.
seasons.evidence: The count takes place from December 14 to January 5

seasons.name: Eagles crowd Wolf Lodge Bay
seasons.note: Bald eagles feeding on the kokanee reach their peak count in late December.
seasons.evidence: from November through February, a migrating population of bald eagles visits the Lake Coeur d' Alene area ... December 20, 2023 ... RECORD COUNT of 409 eagles

seasons.name: Longest night
seasons.note: The winter solstice falls on December 21. After it, the days slowly lengthen.

seasons.name: Goldeneyes on open water
seasons.note: Diving ducks from the north spend the winter on rivers and lakes that stay unfrozen.
seasons.evidence: From November to April, however, Common Goldeneyes are fairly common on both fresh water ... in both the eastern and western lowlands.

seasons.name: Eagles crowd Wolf Lodge Bay
seasons.note: Wintering bald eagles feast on spent kokanee at the north end of Lake Coeur d'Alene.
seasons.evidence: "Eagle numbers will peak between Christmas and New Year's." (Wolf Lodge Bay, Lake Coeur d'Alene)

seasons.name: Windstorms rattle the pines
seasons.note: Early January has brought some of the region's fiercest wind events, with gusts of 70 mph and more.
seasons.evidence: NWS Spokane January history lists high-wind events on January 6, 2007 and January 6, 2009, with gusts of 70 and 78 mph

seasons.name: Snowiest weeks of winter
seasons.note: January is Spokane's snowiest month, averaging about a foot of snow at the airport.
seasons.evidence: Spokane January normals: precipitation 1.97 in, snowfall 12.3 in, the highest of Jan-Mar

seasons.name: Freezing fog rimes the trees
seasons.note: Winter inversions trap fog in the valley and coat branches with rime.
seasons.evidence: NWS Spokane January history: "Extended Freezing Fog" January 16, 2014; "Rime in North Columbia Basin" January 13, 2009

seasons.name: Great horned owls hoot
seasons.note: Male owls hoot at dusk to court mates and claim nest sites in midwinter.
seasons.evidence: WDFW: great horned owls begin pair formation and courtship from mid-January to mid-March; "the male... attempts to attract a female by frequent hooting"

seasons.name: Nights still in the twenties
seasons.note: Late January nights still drop to the mid-20s, the coldest stretch of Spokane's year.
seasons.evidence: Spokane January normal lows 23-26°F; January is the coldest period, with highs near freezing

seasons.name: Willow tips blush with color
seasons.note: Willow and cottonwood twigs brighten along creeks weeks before any leaves open.
seasons.evidence: Feb 2, 2022: willow and poplar trees "start to take color onto the tips of their branches" happening now

seasons.name: Highs climb past forty
seasons.note: Normal afternoon highs in Spokane pass 40°F in early February.
seasons.evidence: Spokane normals: the normal high rises above 40°F beginning in early February (Feb highs 37-44°F)

seasons.name: Red-winged blackbirds flock
seasons.note: Red-winged blackbirds flock back to Spokane-area cattail marshes in early February.
seasons.evidence: "Red-winged blackbirds flocked in the first week of February." - Kristin Stewart, Spokane Audubon Society

seasons.name: Snow fleas on thawing snow
seasons.note: Tiny springtails speckle the snow surface on mild late-winter afternoons.
seasons.evidence: Springtails (snow fleas) "can be seen atop the snow on warm spring days" (eastern WA harbingers, Feb 2022)

seasons.name: Goldfinches turn gold
seasons.note: American goldfinches start trading drab winter feathers for bright yellow, and birdsong picks up.
seasons.evidence: Late winter in Spokane: goldfinches transition from dull winter plumage to bright yellow; "The birds are starting to sing more"

seasons.name: Sagebrush buttercups bloom
seasons.note: The first wild buttercups open on sunny basalt slopes as the snow pulls back.
seasons.evidence: Mar 6, 2017: "10 Facebook friends who've seen their first blooms of 2017 in the past two weeks in Spokane County wild areas"

seasons.name: Ground squirrels wake
seasons.note: Washington ground squirrels and yellow-bellied marmots come out of hibernation.
seasons.evidence: Ground squirrels and yellow-bellied marmots "wake up in March or even late February if it's a mild winter"

seasons.name: Sandhill cranes arrive
seasons.note: Cranes from California stop in eastern Washington to refuel, often passing high over Spokane.
seasons.evidence: Sandhill cranes "start to arrive in Eastern Washington in early March to refuel before flying north"

seasons.name: Bluebirds come home
seasons.note: Western and mountain bluebirds return to claim nest boxes on the Spokane prairies.
seasons.evidence: Western bluebirds "tend to return in March" (eastern Washington biologists, Feb 2022)

seasons.name: Afternoons reach fifty
seasons.note: By mid-March, Spokane's normal daily high passes 50°F.
seasons.evidence: Spokane normals: the normal high "exceeds 50°F by mid-March" (March highs 44-53°F)

seasons.name: Tundra swans pass north
seasons.note: Hundreds of tundra swans rest on Turnbull and Inland Northwest lakes on their way to Alaska.
seasons.evidence: Swans migrate north along inland routes "at the end of winter"; annual Tundra Swan Day held March 20

seasons.name: Tree swallows return
seasons.note: The first swallows of the year skim over the ponds at Turnbull and along the river.
seasons.evidence: Tree Swallows "arrive in March, quite early in the spring"; fairly common by March on the Columbia Plateau

seasons.name: Grass widows open
seasons.note: Purple grass widows are among the first wildflowers on rocky Spokane-area slopes.
seasons.evidence: WSU Extension, Native Plants for Spokane Area Gardens: Grass Widows (Olsynium douglasii) "Blooms early April—June"

seasons.name: Ospreys return to the river
seasons.note: Ospreys come back from their wintering grounds to nest along the Spokane River.
seasons.evidence: "Brad & I found our first osprey of the year on the dike road between Silver and North Silver Lake in Spokane County on March 28."

seasons.name: Swallows skim the ponds
seasons.note: Violet-green and tree swallows hawk insects over Turnbull's wetlands during spring migration.
seasons.evidence: BirdWeb: they "arrive early in spring, especially in eastern Washington, and are one of the first returning migrants"; Turnbull NWR (FWS) spring migration runs "mid-March through mid-May"

seasons.name: Shooting stars nod
seasons.note: Magenta shooting stars bloom in moist meadows and on scabland slopes.
seasons.evidence: WSU Extension, Native Plants for Spokane Area Gardens: Shooting Star (Dodecatheon pulchellum) "Blooms April-May"

seasons.name: Serviceberry in white spray
seasons.note: Serviceberry shrubs flower white across Dishman Hills and Riverside State Park.
seasons.evidence: Spokesman-Review, Apr 27: "NOW is the peak in the golden bloom of arrowleaf balsamroot and the white spray of serviceberry in natural areas around Spokane."

seasons.name: Balsamroot gilds the hills
seasons.note: Arrowleaf balsamroot is in full golden bloom on the sunny slopes below High Drive.
seasons.evidence: Spokesman-Review, Apr 27: "NOW is the peak in the golden bloom of arrowleaf balsamroot ... in natural areas around Spokane."

seasons.name: Last frost
seasons.note: Spokane's average last spring freeze falls in the first week of May, around May 4.
seasons.evidence: Spokesman-Review Weathercatch: average last freeze is "the first week in May," with May 4 given as the average date

seasons.name: Camas turns meadows blue
seasons.note: Blue camas floods wet prairies and Turnbull's meadows, a traditional food of the region's tribes.
seasons.evidence: Spokesman-Review (May 10) on camas near Rathdrum: "It blooms from the middle of April to the middle of June, depending on altitude."

seasons.name: Spokane Falls at full roar
seasons.note: Snowmelt pushes the Spokane River toward its yearly peak through downtown.
seasons.evidence: River peaked May 9, 2023, "close to the average peak"; "The river usually peaks in April or May"

seasons.name: Lilacs crown the Lilac City
seasons.note: Manito's lilacs bloom as the Lilac Festival Torchlight Parade lights up downtown.
seasons.evidence: City of Spokane: "The lilacs are typically in bloom between mid-May and early June." The Torchlight Parade falls on the third Saturday of May.

seasons.name: Wild roses open
seasons.note: Pink Nootka and Woods roses start to open along creeks and fencerows.
seasons.evidence: Kinnikinnick Native Plant Society (north Idaho): "In May through July, large, solitary flowers appear on branch tips."

seasons.name: Syringa scents the canyons
seasons.note: Mock orange, Idaho's state flower, fills basalt draws with a sweet smell.
seasons.evidence: WSU Extension, Native Plants for Spokane Area Gardens: Mock Orange (Philadelphus lewisii) "flowers from late May into July"

seasons.name: Cottonwood fluff drifts
seasons.note: Black cottonwoods along the river release clouds of downy seed.
seasons.evidence: Spokesman-Review: cottonwoods release seeds "usually from the last week of May into about the first two weeks of June"

seasons.name: Strawberries redden on Green Bluff
seasons.note: U-pick strawberry fields open on the Green Bluff farms north of Spokane.
seasons.evidence: Visit Spokane: Green Bluff has "strawberries late May through June"

seasons.name: Hail rides the thunderheads
seasons.note: Mid-June thunderstorms often bring large hail and downpours to the Inland Northwest.
seasons.evidence: NWS Spokane June Weather History: June 10, 2003 "Large Hail Event"; June 13, 2006 "A severe thunderstorm moved through eastern washington and northern Idaho... Large hail was reported"

seasons.name: Ninebark flowers the slopes
seasons.note: Mallow ninebark lays white flower clusters across shady north slopes and forest edges.
seasons.evidence: WSU Extension, Native Plants for Spokane Area Gardens: Ninebark (Physocarpus malvaceus) "Blooms in June"

seasons.name: Sixteen hours of light
seasons.note: At the solstice Spokane gets about 16 hours of daylight, twice December's.
seasons.evidence: "Here in Spokane, the solstice means a day of around 16 hours of sunlight."

seasons.name: Hoopfest fills the streets
seasons.note: The world's largest 3-on-3 basketball tournament takes over downtown courts.
seasons.evidence: Wikipedia: Hoopfest is "traditionally on the last weekend in June" (June 26–27 in 2027)

seasons.name: Cherries ripen on Green Bluff
seasons.note: U-pick cherry season on Green Bluff runs from late June through July.
seasons.evidence: cherries late June through July

seasons.name: Clearest skies of the year
seasons.note: July is Spokane's clearest month, and its skies stay mostly clear about three days in four.
seasons.evidence: July offers the best visibility, with the sky clear, mostly clear, or partly cloudy 75% of the time

seasons.name: Huckleberries purple on Mount Spokane
seasons.note: Huckleberries ripen on the lower slopes first and on the high ridges later in the summer.
seasons.evidence: Two weeks into July ... berries at the Lower Selkirk parking lot were starting to get purple and sweet

seasons.name: Lightning sparks the hills
seasons.note: Dry thunderstorms in midsummer start wildfires across eastern Washington and north Idaho.
seasons.evidence: Lightning ignites the Tin Pan Fire ... Excessively hot and dry conditions (NWS Spokane July weather history)

seasons.name: Sunsets slip earlier
seasons.note: Spokane loses nearly an hour of daylight in July, and sunset moves from 8:51 to 8:25.
seasons.evidence: the length of the day decreases by 56 minutes ... 8:51 PM on July 1 ... 8:25 PM by July 31

seasons.name: Height of summer heat
seasons.note: Normal highs peak near 88°F around August 2, which is the hottest point of Spokane's year.
seasons.evidence: Hottest Day of Year: August 2 reaches 88°F high

seasons.name: Combines roll on the Palouse
seasons.note: Wheat harvest is in full swing across the Palouse's rolling hills in early August.
seasons.evidence: combines are chewing through the amber fields ... The rolling hills of the Palouse are buzzing this time of year (early August)

seasons.name: Smoke veils the sun
seasons.note: Regional wildfire smoke often hangs over Spokane in August and turns the sun orange.
seasons.evidence: Wildfire smoke typically blankets the Spokane area throughout the month of August.

seasons.name: Perseids streak the night
seasons.note: The Perseid meteor shower peaks August 12–13, 2027, and the sky goes dark after moonset.
seasons.evidence: the peak is expected on August 12-13, 2027

seasons.name: Young ospreys take wing
seasons.note: Osprey chicks in the Inland Northwest leave the nest about 60 days after hatching.
seasons.evidence: Fledging occurs about 60 days after hatching ... August 6-17 (2010), August 7 (2011), mid-August (2012-2013) [western Montana]

seasons.name: Rabbitbrush turns gold
seasons.note: Rubber rabbitbrush covers dry scablands and roadsides with pungent yellow blooms.
seasons.evidence: It blooms from August to October and produces pungent-smelling, golden-yellow flowers.

seasons.name: Nighthawks go quiet
seasons.note: Common nighthawks leave eastern Washington at the end of August, with a few lingering.
seasons.evidence: from mid-May through August, but some birds remain into early September

seasons.name: Apples redden on Green Bluff
seasons.note: Green Bluff orchards move into apple harvest, and weekend apple picking runs into October.
seasons.evidence: Harvest season on Green Bluff is generally between August through September.

seasons.name: Summer heat breaks
seasons.note: Spokane's warm season, with daily highs above 78°F, ends around September 12.
seasons.evidence: The warm period runs from June 19 to September 12

seasons.name: Interstate Fair lights up
seasons.note: The Spokane County Interstate Fair runs September 10–19, 2027, in Spokane Valley.
seasons.evidence: 2027 Spokane Fair dates are: September 10-19

seasons.name: Last swallows pass south
seasons.note: Local swallows leave by early September, and the final northern migrants move through late in the month.
seasons.evidence: birds that have bred in Washington leaving the state in late July or early August ... a second wave ... in late September

seasons.name: Elk bugle at dawn
seasons.note: Bull elk bugle most around dawn and dusk during the late-September rut.
seasons.evidence: This peak activity window happens in late September and October ... near dawn and dusk

seasons.name: Ducks crowd Turnbull ponds
seasons.note: Fall waterfowl migration fills the wetlands along the Turnbull auto tour route.
seasons.evidence: Fall migration from September through November ... Most waterfowl can be found on wetlands along the auto tour route

history.name: Open Diary (online diary community)
history.arose: October 20, 1998, United States; founded by Bruce Ableson
history.who: Amateur diarists sharing personal, often anonymous, diaries; by October 2008 more than 561,000 diaries from 77 countries
history.sustained: Early web community with comments and friend-only or public diaries; a first mover among hosted diary sites (the causes are my interpretation; the sourced facts are the founding date and user counts)
history.status: Declined, with two closures: offline February 7, 2014; relaunched January 26, 2018 as a subscription service ($3.99 a month); shutdown announced for January 31, 2026, later extended to February 28, 2026
history.why: The site owners gave financial difficulties as the reason for the 2014 closure. The paid relaunch never won back its earlier scale, and the site was set to close for good in early 2026.

sources.evidence: "It was founded on October 20, 1998" ... "On February 7, 2014, the site went offline." ... "Open Diary re-launched publicly on January 26, 2018" ... "In late 2025, it was announced the site would be shut down on January 31, 2026. This deadline was later extended to February 28."

history.name: Diaryland (hosted web journal)
history.arose: 1999, Canada; created by programmer Andrew Smales
history.who: Teen and young-adult online diarists of the late 1990s and 2000s
history.sustained: Free, simple hosted diary pages with customizable templates (general characterization; the fetched source gives only the founding facts)
history.status: Niche or dormant (not documented). The fetched source gives no user numbers or decline data.
history.why: No sourced decline data. It was probably overtaken by LiveJournal, blogs and social networks, but that is my inference and has no source.

sources.evidence: "Diaryland is an Internet journal service created by Canadian programmer Andrew Smales in 1999."

history.name: LiveJournal
history.arose: April 15, 1999, United States; started by Brad Fitzpatrick
history.who: Friend groups, fandoms and LGBTQ communities, and later a large Russian-speaking user base. As of 2014 it had 10 million monthly uniques in the US.
history.sustained: Friends-list journaling, communities and privacy levels; started "as a way of keeping his high school friends updated"
history.status: Transformed and declined in the West: sold to Russia's SUP Media in 2007; servers moved to Russia in December 2016; terms of service changed to follow Russian law in April 2017. It still runs, mainly in Russia.
history.why: Ownership changes, mass account suspensions in 2007 and security breaches, then the April 2017 terms of service. Those terms banned "political solicitation materials" and "prompted an 'exodus' to alternate platforms" (for example Dreamwidth), especially among LGBTQ users.

sources.evidence: "Brad Fitzpatrick started LiveJournal on April 15, 1999" ... "Six Apart sold LiveJournal to Russian media company SUP Media in 2007" ... "In December 2016, the service relocated its servers to Russia, and in April 2017, LiveJournal changed its terms of service to conform to Russian law."

history.name: Xanga (weblog/diary site)
history.arose: 1999 in the US as a site for book and music reviews; opened to the public in 2000
history.who: Mostly teenagers. In 2006 there were 1.7 million accounts belonging to users under 13, which led to an FTC fine.
history.sustained: Recruitment by email and through GeoCities; free personal blogs popular with teens
history.status: Declined. It failed to raise $60k for 'Xanga 2.0' by mid-July 2013 and "became an un-navigable page in late 2013".
history.why: It lost its money and its users (to Facebook and similar sites, which is my inference). The 2013 crowdfunding drive to save it failed.

sources.evidence: "Xanga began in 1999 as a site for sharing book and music reviews. It became public in 2000" ... "In 2013, Xanga was under threat of shutting down unless it raised $60k by mid-July ... Xanga became an un-navigable page in late 2013."

history.name: Blogger and the blogging boom
history.arose: Launched August 23, 1999 by Pyra Labs (San Francisco); Google bought Pyra, and co-founder Evan Williams left Google in October 2004
history.who: Personal bloggers, diarists and hobbyists; the core of the early-2000s blogging boom
history.sustained: Free, easy publishing, then Google's backing and hosting (moved onto Google servers in 2006)
history.status: Still running with no documented decline in the fetched source. It had redesigns through 2020. Its cultural importance has faded compared with social media (my interpretation, no source).
history.why: The fetched source shows it still operating; no sourced decline figures

sources.evidence: "Pyra Labs launched Blogger on August 23, 1999." ... "Evan Williams, a co-founder of Pyra Labs, left Google in October 2004"

history.name: MySpace personal profiles and blogs
history.arose: August 1, 2003, United States
history.who: Teens, young adults and musicians; peaked at 115 million monthly visitors in April 2008
history.sustained: Customizable profiles, profile blogs and music; bought by News Corp for $580 million in July 2005
history.status: Declined sharply from 2008. Facebook overtook it in the Alexa rankings on April 19, 2008. It sold for about $35 million in 2011, and in March 2019 it lost all content from before 2016.
history.why: Competition from Facebook. The 2019 server migration also destroyed 12 years of user content, more than 50 million songs, which shows how fragile platform-hosted personal archives are.

sources.evidence: "At its peak in April 2008, Myspace had 115 million monthly visitors" ... "On April 19, 2008, Facebook overtook MySpace in Alexa rankings." ... "In March 2019, Myspace lost all content before 2016 after a faulty server migration."

history.name: Tumblr (personal microblogging)
history.arose: February 2007, New York; 75,000 users within two weeks
history.who: Young users and fandom and art communities posting personal reblog-style journals
history.sustained: Easy multimedia posting and reblogging. Yahoo bought it for $1.1 billion (agreed May 20, 2013; closed June 20, 2013).
history.status: Declined but survives. The adult-content ban announced December 3, 2018 (effective December 17) was followed by a 30% loss of traffic (Similarweb). Verizon sold it to Automattic on August 12, 2019 for under $3 million.
history.why: The 2018 content-policy change drove users away; corporate owners also mismanaged it (my interpretation). The sale price was below 0.3% of what Yahoo paid.

sources.evidence: "Tumblr was launched in February 2007" ... "Similarweb estimated Tumblr had lost 30% of its user traffic since December 2018" ... "the sale price was less than $3 million, less than 0.3% of Yahoo's original purchase price"

history.name: PalmPilot / Palm PDAs as planners
history.arose: March 10, 1997, United States; Palm Inc (then a subsidiary of USRobotics, later 3Com)
history.who: Professionals using a digital calendar, contacts and to-do list; more than 1 million units sold by 1998
history.sustained: A pocket digital organizer that synced with a desktop PC; followed by the Palm III (1998) and later models
history.status: Declined and discontinued. After the 2000 IPO the shares lost 90% of their value in just over a year and were at $6.50 by June 2001. HP bought Palm for $1.2 billion (completed July 1, 2010), then on August 18, 2011 announced it would immediately end all Palm/webOS devices.
history.why: Smartphones absorbed the PDA's planner functions (my interpretation), and Palm's finances collapsed. HP dropped webOS in 2011, and HP's own shares then fell 45.4%.

history.name: Evernote (note-taking as a digital commonplace book or journal)
